title: Ruth Perry and the death of single-word Ofsted judgements
narrative_md:
**One headteacher's suicide ended 31 years of Ofsted's most recognisable — and most feared — regulatory signature.**

On 8 January 2023, Ruth Perry, headteacher of Caversham Primary, took her own life while awaiting an Ofsted report downgrading her school from Outstanding to Inadequate. On 2 September 2024, the single-word judgement system she had spent her last weeks dreading was abolished.

The coroner's verdict of 7 December 2023 was unusually direct: Ofsted's inspection 'likely contributed' to Perry's death. Coroner Heidi Connor's prevention of future deaths report concluded that the process was 'rushed, lacked fairness and respect' and that the one-word grade amplified psychological harm out of all proportion to educational reality.

The single-word system — Outstanding, Good, Requires Improvement, Inadequate — had been Ofsted's trademark since 1993. It was efficient for league tables, parents and property markets alike; a 'Good' Ofsted added an estimated 3% to local house prices. But for heads it reduced years of work to a label that could end careers overnight. 94% of heads surveyed after Perry's death said the single grade was 'reductive' or 'harmful.'

Labour's general election manifesto committed to abolition. On 2 September 2024, Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson confirmed single-word judgements were ended immediately for state schools, with the full replacement — a five-part 'report card' covering leadership, behaviour, attendance, inclusion and achievement — to go live in September 2025 following the 'Big Listen' consultation in which 16,000 respondents participated.

Ofsted, led from January 2024 by Sir Martyn Oliver, went further than Phillipson required. The inspectorate committed to a mental-health training programme for inspectors, a 'pause' mechanism where a head signals distress, and a revised complaints process with external review. Oliver publicly apologised to Perry's family.

Critics argue the five-part card is just four-word judgements instead of one, with the same stakes and more dimensions to fear. The NAHT and NEU broadly back reform but warn about workload inflation. Conservative backbenchers argue Labour has 'gone soft on failing schools,' pointing to the early data showing fewer schools triggering formal intervention.

The deeper story is about regulatory capture by simplicity. The single-grade system survived because parents wanted it, estate agents wanted it, and ministers wanted it — the only people who didn't were the ones being judged. It took a death to rebalance that equation. Ruth Perry's sister Julia Waters now runs a reform charity; Perry's school was re-inspected in 2024 and graded Good across the new framework.
